text: Walt, to Mr. Lin, not looking up: "You moved the horse like it was a xiangqi horse again." Mr. Lin: "Because it's better." Walt laughs, which he almost never does.
Walt, to a boy of about twelve who has just taken his queen: "Who taught you that?" The boy: "My abuelo. He's better than me." Walt: "Bring him Saturday." He means it.

Walt, to Harjit, who is watching from the next bench with a paper cup of chai: "You going to play, or just commentate?" Harjit: "In cricket we call this analysis." Walt laughs, which he almost never does.
Gary, on his phone by the fence: "Half the signs at the clinic are in three languages now. I'm just saying the people who've lived here forty years should get a say."
Sunday dinner at Mr. Guo's. Eight people around a lazy Susan, festival budgets on a legal pad between the dishes. He seats you next to the treasurer and says, "Learn from her."
choice1: Stay late and help with the budget.

text: Thursday potluck in the library basement. Ruth seats you with a family who arrived in March and a retired mailman. By dessert the mailman is learning to count to ten in their language.
The association meeting: twelve folding chairs, a coffee urn, forty minutes on the Fifth Street lot. When someone says "those people", Gary changes the subject without looking at you.
choice2: Sit quietly and leave at the break.

text: The joint health fair. Dr. Zhou takes blood pressures at one table, Ruth signs people up for benefits at the next. You spend the morning walking seniors from the center through the library's front door.
Your family group chat, 6:40 a.m.: a forwarded video of agents checking IDs at a subway entrance. Your aunt adds, in all caps, a reminder to carry your passport.
choice2: Mute the chat for the day.

text: The intake form has a new line: 'Citizenship status (required for federal reporting).' The receptionist says quietly, "You can leave it blank. I didn't write that rule."
choice2: Fill it in and hand it back.

text: A local news alert: under the new federal rule, the front desk at the Fifth Street Clinic can now dial a phone interpreter line: Mandarin, Cantonese, or about two hundred other languages. For longer visits, an in-person Mandarin or Cantonese interpreter can be booked for Tuesday mornings. "Ask at the desk, in any language," says the director, Dr. Nadia Haddad.

A local news alert: under the new federal rule, the front desk at the Fifth Street Clinic can now dial a phone interpreter line: Hindi, Punjabi, Malayalam, or about two hundred other languages. For longer visits, an in-person Hindi and Punjabi interpreter can be booked for Tuesday mornings. "Ask at the desk, in any language," says the director, Dr. Nadia Haddad.
Dr. Zhou is pinning a notice to the board: 'New: free help with citizenship applications. Library and Center, together.' She steps back to check it's straight.

Morning radio: a Guatemalan family two neighborhoods over was detained at a routine check-in. Their kids went to school at PS 21, where half the kids in your building go. The principal, Karen Novak, says counselors will be in every classroom today.

Morning radio, the governor's call-in hour. Dale Whitaker says state troopers will "help our federal partners" with ID checks on the interstate. A caller asks about people whose applications are still pending. "If your paperwork's in order, you've got nothing to worry about."

A letter is taped inside the reception window, signed by the director, Dr. Nadia Haddad: 'This clinic does not ask about immigration status and does not share your records with anyone who is not treating you.' Someone has underlined 'anyone' in blue pen.
choice1: Take a photo of it for your family.

text: A note from PS 21 goes round your building's group chat. The principal, Karen Novak: parent-teacher night will have interpreters for the five languages families asked for most, and a phone line for the rest: "just tell the front desk which, a week ahead." Someone replies: "Finally. Last year I nodded for an hour."
choice1: Forward it to your cousin with kids.

text: Dana waves you over and slides a book across the desk: a cookbook from the Sichuan place on Grand that closed in 2019. "Found it in donations. You said you missed their fish."
Dana waves you over and slides a book across the desk: a cookbook from the Oaxacan place on Fifth that closed in 2019. "Found it in donations. You said you missed their mole."
Dana waves you over and slides a book across the desk: a cookbook from the Kerala place on Fifth that closed in 2019. "Found it in donations. You said you missed their fish curry."
Mrs. Chen hands you an apron. "Seniors' lunch, sixty people, two volunteers sick. You fold, I'll boil." The dumpling wrappers are already counted into stacks of twenty.
Mr. Guo, to the room, not quite to you: "Some young people come here once a month, like visiting a museum." A couple of the aunties look at their teacups.
choice2: Say nothing and help stack chairs.

text: Jia drops a container of frozen dumplings on your desk. "My mom made two hundred. I'm outsourcing. Don't tell her, she'll ask what you thought."
A manager from another team, after your presentation: "Your English is really good, by the way. Where are you from originally?" You've lived in this city longer than he has.
Mr. Lin has drawn a xiangqi river in chalk across the stone board and is showing Walt how the elephant can't cross it. Walt says it's a stupid rule. He keeps playing.
choice1: Pull up a seat and coach Walt.

text: A voice message from your mom: she's making zongzi this weekend and wants to know how many to save you. Then, as an afterthought, whether you've called your grandmother.
A voice message from your mom: she's making tamales this weekend and wants to know how many to save you. Then, as an afterthought, whether you've called your grandmother.
A voice message from your mom: she's making samosas for your cousin's engagement this weekend and wants to know how many to save you. Then, as an afterthought, whether you've called your grandmother.

Nine a.m. on the roof. Dana has two folding chairs, a thermos, and an empty pot with 3B written on it in marker, waiting for spring. Mr. Ortiz comes up at ten and tells you both the pots are in the wrong corner.
choice1: Stay and help move the pots.
choice2: Finish your coffee and head down.

text: A knock at the door. Dana, in slippers, holding a foil tray: "Mr. Ortiz made lasagna for twelve and decided it was my problem. Now half of it is yours. Bring the tray back whenever."
A knock. Mrs. Chen from 4A, with a plastic bag: two egg tarts and a pear. "Golden Wheat gave thirteen again. You are the thirteenth. Eat them sitting down."
choice1: Thank her and ask about Kevin.
choice2: Take the bag and say goodnight.

text: Your phone: Dana. "Sorry, is this weird? There were two men in jackets asking the super who lives in 2C. He didn't tell them. I just wanted to check you were home."

First-Friday merchants' breakfast in the back room of the diner on Fifth. Frank introduces you to the dry cleaner, a bank manager and the city's parking man as "my friend from Elm Street." Nobody asks where you're from.
choice1: Stay and help him hand out flyers.

text: Sunday at the Fongs': twenty soccer families, one grill, Alan's wife in charge of all of it. The parents talk about college visits. Someone's grandmother sits by the door, and Alan brings her a plate without being asked.
choice1: Stay and help clean the grill.

text: Chamber breakfast, seven a.m., a hotel ballroom with half the lights on. Ray works the room in a good suit and steers you toward a banker. "Tell him about the hall's roof fund," he says. "In numbers. They like numbers."
choice2: Eat a muffin and slip out.

text: Thursday at the library: a table for library cards, a legal aid lawyer in the meeting room, Sra. Reyes's sister's pan dulce gone by seven. Ruth and Pilar run it like they've done it for years. They have.

Saturday at the Mendozas': birria, the Club's board, a ledger on the kitchen table between the bowls. Don Aurelio seats you beside the treasurer, a woman of seventy. "Watch her. She hasn't lost a dollar since 1989."
choice1: Stay late and go through the ledger.

text: Pancake breakfast at the Rotary hall. Anil runs the griddle in a borrowed apron. The parents talk travel teams and orthodontists. Someone asks where you work, not where you're from.
choice1: Take a turn at the griddle.

text: Lantern night at the library. Two long tables, thirty kids, glue everywhere. A boy from Meena's group explains diyas to a girl from Ruth's homework club, very seriously. She makes hers purple.
choice1: Stay to scrape glue off the tables.
choice2: Leave once the lanterns are lit.

text: Sunday dinner at the Deshpandes'. Puran poli, the building committee, the roof quote spread across the dining table. Mr. Deshpande hands you a calculator. "Check my numbers. Everyone else is afraid to."
Sra. Reyes hands you a box cutter. "Pantry day, two volunteers missing. You open, I sort." The cans go in rows by the kitchen door: beans, tomatoes, one lonely can of cranberry sauce.
Don Ernesto, at his folding table, to a young man holding a flyer: "A notario here is not a lawyer. This person wants two thousand dollars for a form that is free. Sit. We will read it together."
A knock. Sra. Reyes from 2A, holding a plate under foil. "Daniel didn't come for dinner. His loss. Bring the plate back, it's my good one. And the shower is still dripping."
choice1: Thank her and promise to fix the drip.
choice2: Take the plate and say goodnight.

text: Mrs. Nair presses a steel tiffin into your hands, still warm. "Onam lunch leftovers. Rice, sambar, payasam. Don't carry it sideways. And bring back the box."
choice1: Thank her and ask about Anjali.

text: Harjit, phone propped on a water bottle, explaining cricket to Walt. "Six balls, one over." Walt: "Why's it called an over?" Harjit: "Because then it's over." Walt sits down anyway.
A knock. Mrs. Nair from 3C, in scrubs, holding a package. "Yours. It came to my door. Also, the radiator is doing the pressure cooker thing again. Is yours?"
